subject: English
summaryPoints: Modal verbs of obligation and necessity differentiate the source of requirement: 'must' signals subjective obligation from the speaker, while 'have to' indicates external laws, guidelines, or conditions.
'Mustn't' (must not) is an explicit marker of prohibition stating that an action is forbidden; it cannot be replaced by 'don't have to'.
'Don't have to' and 'need not' (needn't) express absence of obligation, stating that a task is optional and non-compulsory.
Suffixes '-ate' and '-ise/-ize' are derivational affixes that convert nouns and adjectives into verbs (e.g., 'capacitate', 'prioritize', 'generalize').
Suffixes '-ment' and '-tion' are nominalizing morphemes that convert verbs into nouns denoting states, actions, or results (e.g., 'amazement', 'punishment', 'action', 'dissatisfaction').

High-yield phrasal verbs formed with 'come' and 'close' include 'come about' (happen/occur), 'come across' (find by chance), 'come apart' (break into pieces), 'close down' (permanently cease operations), and 'close off' (barricade/block).

formulas.label: Absence of Obligation Formula
formulas.expr: Subject + don't/doesn't + have to + V1(base)  OR  Subject + need not + V1(base)

formulas.label: Verb-Forming Suffix Patterns
formulas.expr: Noun/Adjective + -ize/-ise  ->  Verb (e.g., priority -> prioritize)  |  Noun/Adj + -ate  ->  Verb (e.g., active -> activate)

formulas.label: Noun-Forming Suffix Patterns
formulas.expr: Verb + -ment  ->  Noun (e.g., measure -> measurement)  |  Verb + -tion/-ation  ->  Noun (e.g., satisfy -> satisfaction)

examTip: Note the syntax of 'need': when used as a modal verb of absence of obligation, 'need not' takes a bare infinitive without 'to' (e.g., 'You need not come'). When used as an ordinary lexical verb, it requires 'to' (e.g., 'You do not need to come').

keyDefinitions.definition: A modality expressing that a person is under no compulsion, necessity, or requirement to perform an act.
An authoritative ban or legal bar that renders an activity impermissible.
An affix attached to the end of a word stem that creates a new lexical item, commonly modifying its grammatical word class.
A historical form of complete ownership where an individual is treated as legal property, bought, sold, and coerced to labor without pay.
